before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.
before.explanation: Carrier input is followed through entry, expression, survival and expansion without specifying a final in-body cell dose. before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.
before.explanation: Each card retains its product, specimen, controls, denominator, time and uncertainty and asks for the next missing measurement. before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

before.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.
before.explanation: Each card retains its product, specimen, controls, denominator, time and uncertainty and asks for the next missing measurement. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

points.requirement: Distinguish integration-deficient lentiviral designs from ordinary integrating designs and self-inactivating vectors from nonintegrating vectors.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three design labels are easy to confuse. Replication-defective means the delivered particle lacks the machinery to propagate as an ordinary virus, which does not replace testing: FDA guidance sets out testing of retroviral vector products, lentiviral ones included, for replication-competent virus during manufacture and in patient follow-up. Self-inactivating means regulatory sequences in the long terminal repeats are disabled: in the original design a 133 base-pair deletion in the U3 region of the 3' repeat was copied to the 5' repeat after reverse transcription and integration, and the vector still expressed from an internal promoter in rat brain and eye (Miyoshi and colleagues). It does not mean the cassette cannot integrate. Integration-deficient means integrase is mutated: with a class 1 integrase mutation, residual integration was lower than with intact integrase by a factor of 500 to 1,250, expression was transient in dividing cell lines and long-lived in non-dividing neural cultures and in mouse brain, consistent with an episomal genome (Philippe and colleagues). The name does not promise zero integration or lasting expression in dividing cells such as T cells.
evidence.explanation: Integration-deficient and self-inactivating lentiviral designs are explicitly different; disabling LTR regulation does not prevent integration. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Where the DNA sits was measured in different systems. In sequential muscle biopsies taken 3 and 12 months after an intramuscular AAV vector expressing alpha-1 antitrypsin, most vector DNA was double-stranded circular episomes, and clones recovered from the biopsies were transcriptionally active (Schnepp and colleagues; abstract read, full text not retrievable). After partial hepatectomy in mice, extrachromosomal genomes were the main form behind liver expression and in most cases no more than about 10 per cent of stably transduced genomes had integrated, although one of three mice at a higher dose had 67 per cent integrated genomes (Nakai and colleagues). evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
This retrospective analysis used samples collected prospectively in I-SPY2 from 84 high-risk early breast-cancer patients receiving standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without the AKT inhibitor MK-2206. The cohort included hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive and triple-negative disease. Personalised panels tracked up to 16 mutations from pretreatment tumour sequencing. Blood collection was planned before treatment, three weeks after starting paclitaxel, between chemotherapy blocks and after chemotherapy before surgery. The analysis used 291 of 336 potential plasma samples; availability differed by draw.

The authors reported ctDNA detection in 61 of 84 at baseline (73%), followed by 35%, 14% and 9% at successive draws. These are not four proportions with a common denominator of 84. In the joint post-treatment pathology and outcome analysis of 60 patients, all 17 with the specified pathological complete response were ctDNA-negative. Among 43 without that response, the six ctDNA-positive patients had greater distant-recurrence risk than the 37 negative patients: hazard ratio 10.4, 95% confidence interval 2.3 to 46.6. Comparing ctDNA-negative non-pCR patients with pCR patients gave hazard ratio 1.4, interval 0.15 to 13.5; that wide interval does not establish equivalence. Median survival follow-up was 4.8 years. This assay analysis did not randomise a blood-guided treatment strategy.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Complete abstract plus targeted methods, availability and 60-person joint-analysis paragraphs. The exact final-draw denominator for the reported 9% remains unverified.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The assay required at least two detected somatic variants for a positive call and selected 12 to 16 targets per person, with a median of 16. A fixed personalised panel is therefore neither a complete tumour genome nor a one-molecule guarantee. The four blood collection moments and the available specimens belong beside each reported percentage; the joint 60-person analysis is a separate denominator from the whole cohort of 84. The MRI companion report asks how blood and functional tumour volume relate, rather than supplying another independent treatment-strategy trial.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:

For solid tumours, plasma assays can look for selected tumour-associated DNA features, with results interpreted under their specimen, input, target and calling rules. Clinical usefulness belongs to a defined strategy: the cancer setting, assay, timing, triggering result, action and comparator. evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The two-window comparison is about scope. evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

points.requirement: Verify the Annals of Oncology 84-person high-risk mixed-subtype neoadjuvant study, serial sampling and up-to-16-mutation tumour-informed design; keep it distinct from the companion MRI paper.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
This retrospective analysis used samples collected prospectively in I-SPY2 from 84 high-risk early breast-cancer patients receiving standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without the AKT inhibitor MK-2206. The cohort included hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive and triple-negative disease. Personalised panels tracked up to 16 mutations from pretreatment tumour sequencing. Blood collection was planned before treatment, three weeks after starting paclitaxel, between chemotherapy blocks and after chemotherapy before surgery. The analysis used 291 of 336 potential plasma samples; availability differed by draw.

The authors reported ctDNA detection in 61 of 84 at baseline (73%), followed by 35%, 14% and 9% at successive draws. These are not four proportions with a common denominator of 84. In the joint post-treatment pathology and outcome analysis of 60 patients, all 17 with the specified pathological complete response were ctDNA-negative. Among 43 without that response, the six ctDNA-positive patients had greater distant-recurrence risk than the 37 negative patients: hazard ratio 10.4, 95% confidence interval 2.3 to 46.6. Comparing ctDNA-negative non-pCR patients with pCR patients gave hazard ratio 1.4, interval 0.15 to 13.5; that wide interval does not establish equivalence. Median survival follow-up was 4.8 years. This assay analysis did not randomise a blood-guided treatment strategy.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Complete abstract plus targeted methods, availability and 60-person joint-analysis paragraphs. The exact final-draw denominator for the reported 9% remains unverified.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The assay required at least two detected somatic variants for a positive call and selected 12 to 16 targets per person, with a median of 16. A fixed personalised panel is therefore neither a complete tumour genome nor a one-molecule guarantee. The four blood collection moments and the available specimens belong beside each reported percentage; the joint 60-person analysis is a separate denominator from the whole cohort of 84. The MRI companion report asks how blood and functional tumour volume relate, rather than supplying another independent treatment-strategy trial.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Targeted assay methods and joint-analysis passages plus complete abstracts. The 60-person joint analysis differs from the 84-person parent cohort; the MRI report is a companion analysis.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

points.requirement: Distinguish integration-deficient lentiviral designs from ordinary integrating designs and self-inactivating vectors from nonintegrating vectors.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three design labels are easy to confuse. Replication-defective means the delivered particle lacks the machinery to propagate as an ordinary virus, which does not replace testing: FDA guidance sets out testing of retroviral vector products, lentiviral ones included, for replication-competent virus during manufacture and in patient follow-up. Self-inactivating means regulatory sequences in the long terminal repeats are disabled: in the original design a 133 base-pair deletion in the U3 region of the 3' repeat was copied to the 5' repeat after reverse transcription and integration, and the vector still expressed from an internal promoter in rat brain and eye (Miyoshi and colleagues). It does not mean the cassette cannot integrate. Integration-deficient means integrase is mutated: with a class 1 integrase mutation, residual integration was lower than with intact integrase by a factor of 500 to 1,250, expression was transient in dividing cell lines and long-lived in non-dividing neural cultures and in mouse brain, consistent with an episomal genome (Philippe and colleagues). The name does not promise zero integration or lasting expression in dividing cells such as T cells.
evidence.explanation: Integration-deficient and self-inactivating lentiviral designs are explicitly different; disabling LTR regulation does not prevent integration. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Where the DNA sits was measured in different systems. In sequential muscle biopsies taken 3 and 12 months after an intramuscular AAV vector expressing alpha-1 antitrypsin, most vector DNA was double-stranded circular episomes, and clones recovered from the biopsies were transcriptionally active (Schnepp and colleagues; abstract read, full text not retrievable). After partial hepatectomy in mice, extrachromosomal genomes were the main form behind liver expression and in most cases no more than about 10 per cent of stably transduced genomes had integrated, although one of three mice at a higher dose had 67 per cent integrated genomes (Nakai and colleagues). That shows the usual behaviour of the tested vectors in those tissues, not that integration never happens, and persistent DNA does not show an intact cassette, enough protein or a surviving functional cell: in the muscle study the episomal inverted terminal repeats ranged from fully intact to severely deleted, so counting vector DNA is a different measurement from showing a working cassette.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

Collection, transport, manufacture, testing, release and clinical readiness contribute to that interval; culture time alone does not describe it. evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

points.requirement: Distinguish integration-deficient lentiviral designs from ordinary integrating designs and self-inactivating vectors from nonintegrating vectors.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Three design labels are easy to confuse. Replication-defective means the delivered particle lacks the machinery to propagate as an ordinary virus, which does not replace testing: FDA guidance sets out testing of retroviral vector products, lentiviral ones included, for replication-competent virus during manufacture and in patient follow-up. Self-inactivating means regulatory sequences in the long terminal repeats are disabled: in the original design a 133 base-pair deletion in the U3 region of the 3' repeat was copied to the 5' repeat after reverse transcription and integration, and the vector still expressed from an internal promoter in rat brain and eye (Miyoshi and colleagues). It does not mean the cassette cannot integrate. Integration-deficient means integrase is mutated: with a class 1 integrase mutation, residual integration was lower than with intact integrase by a factor of 500 to 1,250, expression was transient in dividing cell lines and long-lived in non-dividing neural cultures and in mouse brain, consistent with an episomal genome (Philippe and colleagues). The name does not promise zero integration or lasting expression in dividing cells such as T cells.
evidence.explanation: Integration-deficient and self-inactivating lentiviral designs are explicitly different; disabling LTR regulation does not prevent integration. evidence.supportingExcerpt: A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Where the DNA sits was measured in different systems. In sequential muscle biopsies taken 3 and 12 months after an intramuscular AAV vector expressing alpha-1 antitrypsin, most vector DNA was double-stranded circular episomes, and clones recovered from the biopsies were transcriptionally active (Schnepp and colleagues; abstract read, full text not retrievable). After partial hepatectomy in mice, extrachromosomal genomes were the main form behind liver expression and in most cases no more than about 10 per cent of stably transduced genomes had integrated, although one of three mice at a higher dose had 67 per cent integrated genomes (Nakai and colleagues). That shows the usual behaviour of the tested vectors in those tissues, not that integration never happens, and persistent DNA does not show an intact cassette, enough protein or a surviving functional cell: in the muscle study the episomal inverted terminal repeats ranged from fully intact to severely deleted, so counting vector DNA is a different measurement from showing a working cassette.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Some gene delivery systems, including the viral vectors used to make engineered T cells and to correct inherited immune disorders in blood stem cells, insert a genetic cassette into the cell's genome. Integration is the event; insertional mutagenesis is a consequential change that the event causes, such as interrupting a gene or altering the activity of a nearby one. Integration alone does not establish a harmful biological consequence. A cell that gains a growth advantage passes the insertion to its descendants and a clone expands, but a growing clone is not a diagnosis of cancer, because a useful therapeutic response can also expand a clone. FDA's long-term follow-up guidance for gene therapy (January 2020) explains why the question is taken seriously: the biological activity of retroviral vectors and transposon elements is imparted by an integration event, such integration is in general not directed to specific sites, and that raises the potential for disruption of critical host genes or activation of proto-oncogenes near the site, and so the risk of malignancy. A nonviral transposon is therefore also an integrating system, and genome editing can produce its own undesirable changes with a risk of malignancy, which is a separate mechanism from vector insertion.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

Source scope: Complete Moss abstract and targeted workflow guidance; definitions and finite-sample scope, without certifying older product or collection claims.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. Both samples are called detected, but the second is below the assay's reliable quantitation range. The printed estimates fall by two-thirds; they do not establish that the cancer volume fell by two-thirds. Retain the qualifying calls and uncertainty, because shedding and background DNA can change the signal. A second method reporting molecules per millilitre cannot simply be placed on this fraction scale. Even a matching unit label does not establish matching calibration. Keeping serial methods and input comparable helps interpretation without removing biological variation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The two-window comparison is about scope. A finite plasma aliquot contains extracellular DNA, of which tumour-derived fragments may be one part; breast MRI observes regional, sequence-dependent features rather than individual cancer cells. Contrast enhancement reflects vascular and contrast-delivery behaviour as well as the acquisition protocol; it is not a one-to-one viable-cell count. In the 84-person I-SPY2 MRI pilot, functional tumour volume summed voxels meeting 70% enhancement about two and a half minutes after contrast, inside a manually drawn box around the lesion. A camera-and-stream analogy illustrates those two sampled views without promising that every tumour sheds DNA. Keep the imaging method visible: mammography uses X-rays, ultrasound uses sound, and PET/CT combines tracer-distribution images with anatomical CT images. A formal response category needs its framework, comparison timepoint and findings outside a selected lesion measurement. None of these measurements is an interchangeable all-body tumour-cell number.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

Source scope: Conditional Poisson arithmetic: independent loci, retained-target calling, target-allele probability and copy-number assumptions are explicit, not a clinical false-negative rate.

points.requirement: Verify the Annals of Oncology 84-person high-risk mixed-subtype neoadjuvant study, serial sampling and up-to-16-mutation tumour-informed design; keep it distinct from the companion MRI paper.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
This retrospective analysis used samples collected prospectively in I-SPY2 from 84 high-risk early breast-cancer patients receiving standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without the AKT inhibitor MK-2206. The cohort included hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive and triple-negative disease. Personalised panels tracked up to 16 mutations from pretreatment tumour sequencing. Blood collection was planned before treatment, three weeks after starting paclitaxel, between chemotherapy blocks and after chemotherapy before surgery. The analysis used 291 of 336 potential plasma samples; availability differed by draw.

The authors reported ctDNA detection in 61 of 84 at baseline (73%), followed by 35%, 14% and 9% at successive draws. These are not four proportions with a common denominator of 84. In the joint post-treatment pathology and outcome analysis of 60 patients, all 17 with the specified pathological complete response were ctDNA-negative. Among 43 without that response, the six ctDNA-positive patients had greater distant-recurrence risk than the 37 negative patients: hazard ratio 10.4, 95% confidence interval 2.3 to 46.6. Comparing ctDNA-negative non-pCR patients with pCR patients gave hazard ratio 1.4, interval 0.15 to 13.5; that wide interval does not establish equivalence. Median survival follow-up was 4.8 years. This assay analysis did not randomise a blood-guided treatment strategy.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Complete abstract plus targeted methods, availability and 60-person joint-analysis paragraphs. The exact final-draw denominator for the reported 9% remains unverified.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The assay required at least two detected somatic variants for a positive call and selected 12 to 16 targets per person, with a median of 16. A fixed personalised panel is therefore neither a complete tumour genome nor a one-molecule guarantee. The four blood collection moments and the available specimens belong beside each reported percentage; the joint 60-person analysis is a separate denominator from the whole cohort of 84. The MRI companion report asks how blood and functional tumour volume relate, rather than supplying another independent treatment-strategy trial.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Targeted assay methods and joint-analysis passages plus complete abstracts. The 60-person joint analysis differs from the 84-person parent cohort; the MRI report is a companion analysis.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Residual-disease testing asks whether a qualifying disease signal is present after treatment in a specified sample. For solid tumours, plasma assays can look for selected tumour-associated DNA features, with results interpreted under their specimen, input, target and calling rules. Analytical detection, clinical detection in a population and recurrence association are different performance questions. A valid negative does not establish absence of every cancer cell.

Clinical usefulness belongs to a defined strategy: the cancer setting, assay, timing, triggering result, action and comparator. Evidence for genotyping, an approved indication or a strategy in another cancer does not automatically settle an early-breast-cancer question. The dated trial examples below retain their studied populations. More frequent detection, molecular clearance or favourable prognosis in treated negative groups does not by itself show improved patient outcomes or safe treatment omission.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Separate three test jobs. Tumour-informed monitoring asks whether selected known tumour features reached the plasma sample; it need not discover new variants outside that list. Reference-free monitoring asks whether a qualifying cancer-associated signal is present without prior tumour sequencing; it need not return a complete genomic profile. Plasma genomic profiling asks which covered alterations are detectable; it does not automatically have a dedicated low-signal monitoring assay's sensitivity. Real methods can combine features. Methylation and fragment-pattern analysis need not produce a mutation list, and a captured circulating tumour cell is a cell, a different object from cell-free DNA fragments.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Consider a fictional assay estimating tumour fraction at 6 parts per million (PPM) and then 2 PPM. evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a fictional model, an evaluated aliquot supplies 4,500 independent amplifiable opportunities at one locus, each with a target-allele probability of 1 in 10,000. The expected target count is 0.45. If target counts follow a Poisson distribution, the chance of no target is exp(-0.45), 63.8%. Twenty independent loci with the same opportunity count and probability give an expected total of 9 and exp(-9), 0.012%, for none. Independence, equal recovery and one retained target being sufficient are assumptions of this model. These are not measured clinical false-negative rates. A tumour-DNA fraction cannot simply replace the target-allele probability without assumptions about copy number, variant multiplicity and which tumour clones carry the variant. More reads cannot recover an original molecule absent from the aliquot.

points.requirement: Verify the Annals of Oncology 84-person high-risk mixed-subtype neoadjuvant study, serial sampling and up-to-16-mutation tumour-informed design; keep it distinct from the companion MRI paper.

evidence.supportingExcerpt:
This retrospective analysis used samples collected prospectively in I-SPY2 from 84 high-risk early breast-cancer patients receiving standard neoadjuvant chemotherapy with or without the AKT inhibitor MK-2206. The cohort included hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, HER2-positive and triple-negative disease. Personalised panels tracked up to 16 mutations from pretreatment tumour sequencing. Blood collection was planned before treatment, three weeks after starting paclitaxel, between chemotherapy blocks and after chemotherapy before surgery. The analysis used 291 of 336 potential plasma samples; availability differed by draw.

The authors reported ctDNA detection in 61 of 84 at baseline (73%), followed by 35%, 14% and 9% at successive draws. These are not four proportions with a common denominator of 84. In the joint post-treatment pathology and outcome analysis of 60 patients, all 17 with the specified pathological complete response were ctDNA-negative. Among 43 without that response, the six ctDNA-positive patients had greater distant-recurrence risk than the 37 negative patients: hazard ratio 10.4, 95% confidence interval 2.3 to 46.6. Comparing ctDNA-negative non-pCR patients with pCR patients gave hazard ratio 1.4, interval 0.15 to 13.5; that wide interval does not establish equivalence. Median survival follow-up was 4.8 years. This assay analysis did not randomise a blood-guided treatment strategy.
evidence.explanation: The high-risk mixed-subtype 84-person assay analysis, four planned times and personalised targets are present and separated from its MRI companion. Source scope: Complete abstract plus targeted methods, availability and 60-person joint-analysis paragraphs. The exact final-draw denominator for the reported 9% remains unverified.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The assay required at least two detected somatic variants for a positive call and selected 12 to 16 targets per person, with a median of 16. A fixed personalised panel is therefore neither a complete tumour genome nor a one-molecule guarantee. The four blood collection moments and the available specimens belong beside each reported percentage; the joint 60-person analysis is a separate denominator from the whole cohort of 84. The MRI companion report asks how blood and functional tumour volume relate, rather than supplying another independent treatment-strategy trial.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A surrogate is a measured outcome used in place of a direct clinical-benefit outcome, with evidence needed for that substitution in the intended setting. Two relationships must be separated: people with a favourable marker may have better outcomes, while treatments that improve that marker may or may not improve the outcome. The first is a prognostic association; the second concerns agreement between treatment effects across suitable randomised comparisons. A treatment can change another pathway, later disease or toxicity as well as the marker. Validation is specific to disease, treatment context and intended outcome. Even a pathology or imaging response does not capture every benefit and harm.

points.requirement: Ladan and colleagues tested whether breast-cancer tissue slices could predict response to chemotherapy given before surgery ([Ladan 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10542784/)). Biopsy cores were cut into thin slices and exposed for 3 days to 5-fluorouracil, doxorubicin and the active form of cyclophosphamide. Each tumor was called sensitive, intermediate or resistant. The comparison was the tumor's size change on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after four cycles of anthracycline-containing chemotherapy, measured with [Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST)](/wiki/education/concepts/measurement/imaging/response-criteria) but grouped by the study's own cutoffs: "sensitive" meant more than 50% shrinkage, a stricter bar than RECIST's 30% for partial response. Before starting, the team set a target of at least 55% agreement.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Primary preparation example. Ladan used 300 micrometre slices and three-day exposure in a defined anthracycline-based assay, measuring morphology, proliferation and apoptosis. Diffusion into slices differs from vascular delivery; host metabolic activation, clearance, organ toxicity and new immune recruitment were not recreated. Preparation injury, poor viability, uneven diffusion, changing populations and non-tumour signal can invalidate interpretation. A failed culture is not evidence of clinical resistance. Contamination is another reason for assay failure; short-term response does not establish durable elimination, systemic safety or benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A trial defines primary, secondary and exploratory outcomes and how they are measured and analysed. The primary question informs design, sample size and testing; having a secondary endpoint does not by itself establish whether it was adequately powered or met a prespecified testing rule.
